title: Is Understanding Just Remembering in Disguise?
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick takes Dan Willingham's line that understanding is 'remembering in disguise' and reads it through cognitive load theory's concept of element interactivity, the degree to which the parts of a body of knowledge change each other's meaning. He argues that difficulty lives in the knowledge itself before it lives in the learner: a list of French nouns can be learned item by item, whereas the terms, signs and rules of an equation only mean something together. This produces a paradox in which a novice can hold every element in memory and still understand nothing, yet the relations cannot be taught to someone who lacks the elements to relate. Hendrick concludes that 'teaching for understanding' names a destination rather than a method, because understanding is a property of well-arranged knowledge and not a generic skill. The practical consequence is that instructional design, meaning the careful sequencing of parts into a coherent whole, is where understanding is actually built, and the supposed opposition between rote memorising and understanding is false.
points: Element interactivity describes the content rather than the learner: the more the elements of a topic depend on one another, the heavier the load on working memory.
A student can recall every fact about a topic and still not understand it, because understanding is the relations between elements, not the elements alone.
Those relations cannot be taught to a pupil who lacks the underlying knowledge, so you cannot connect dots you do not have.
'Teaching for understanding' sounds like a method but is really a destination that differs for every topic; there are no generic 'understanding skills'.
Because memorising and understanding are interacting elements of the same process, sequencing and instructional design are where understanding is won.
quotes: The crucial aspect of this idea is not that understanding is the mere recall of disparate element but rather the way we recombine and reassemble them to form meaning.
For example, the student who can list all those elements of knowledge about WWI but cannot say why any one of them mattered.
the relations cannot be taught to the pupil who doesn’t have the elements in their memory because they have nothing to connect. You can’t connect the dots if you don’t have any.
As Christine Counsell reminds us, knowledge “is not information. It is not comprised of lists of facts, but of connections and relationships held together by structures, textures and flows.

Expertise is ultimately the particular arrangement of knowledge. Nine separate elements unmoored from the substrate of understanding, leads to confusion and it is that at the end of the day is what separates a novice from an expert.

You cannot teach “understanding skills” any more than you can teach remembering. You can only teach the parts, carefully curated, in an order that working memory can tolerate, with the broader aim that we will arrange for them to be combined and “understood” at a later date.
Ultimately the opposition between rote memorising and understanding is misleading. They are two interacting elements themselves. You can’t have one without the other.
